item.title: Maybe You're Not Breaking Down. Maybe You're Molting
item.description:
Growth Mindset

Maybe You're Not Breaking Down. Maybe You're Molting

Personal Perspective: What I learned from the birds.

Posted August 8, 2026

Motivational speakers love butterflies. So do gurus and pastors and coaches. Butterflies offer a stirring metaphor for the potential of human transformation. You disappear into a chrysalis, do some mysterious inner work, and emerge shockingly upgraded, effortlessly beautiful, and ready to soar. It's a lovely image, but it has one glaring problem: Almost none of us experience change that way. Most of us don't wake up one morning with a brand-new identity. We wake up feeling oddly uncomfortable in the old one.

Susan Levinson
Source: Susan Levinson/Used with permission

I recently stumbled onto a metaphor that feels much closer to real life while recording my podcast, Fifty Words for Snow. Every week, my friend Emily John Garcés and I invite a guest on to introduce us to a word from a language other than English or from the vernacular of a particular culture. The podcast is built around the idea that language gives us new ways of seeing ourselves, and sometimes a single word quietly rearranges how we think. This week, our guest, Ballona Wetlands tour guide and bird expert Susan Levinson, introduced us to the word molt: the process by which an animal sheds an outer layer that can no longer serve it.

The more I learned about molting, the more I wondered why we don't use it as our primary metaphor for change. Snakes shed their skin. Tarantulas crawl out of an entire exoskeleton. Deer lose their antlers. Birds replace their feathers because feathers cannot repair themselves. Once a feather has become worn, there is no polishing it or patching it. The only way to get a new feather is to let the old one go. That strikes me as a much more honest description of what psychological growth often feels like than the butterfly model.

The Problem With Self-Improvement

I realized how different this is from the way we usually think about psychological growth. We tend to imagine that becoming healthier means adding things to ourselves. More confidence. Better boundaries. Greater resilience. Improved communication. A calmer nervous system. We picture ourselves as home renovation projects, constantly installing upgrades.

But what if some of the most important growth doesn't come from adding anything at all? What if it comes from shedding? What if the next version of ourselves isn't hidden underneath a new skill but underneath an old habit we're finally ready to release? That possibility feels both less glamorous and much more honest.

Looking Scruffy

One of my favorite things I learned about birds is that they don't molt all at once. If they suddenly lost every feather, many of them wouldn't be able to fly. Instead, they lose a few feathers and grow a few feathers. During that time, they often look a little ragged. A little uneven. A little less magnificent than the nature documentaries would have us believe.

I found that oddly comforting because psychological change has always made me feel scruffy. There is an awkward stretch where the old way of being no longer fits, but the new way hasn't settled in yet. You're less certain. Less polished. Less fluent. From the outside, it can look as though you're regressing, when in fact you're simply in the middle of replacing something that can no longer carry you.

The Feathers We Keep Repairing

It also struck me that many of our emotional habits resemble old feathers. They were once exactly what we needed. People-pleasing may have kept the peace in a chaotic family. Perfectionism may have earned us praise. Constant productivity may have helped us feel safe in an unpredictable world. These strategies deserve a little gratitude. They got us here.

The trouble begins when we assume that because something once protected us, it must protect us forever. We become remarkably loyal to coping strategies that have quietly outlived their usefulness. Instead of letting them fall away, we spend years trying to repair them. We become experts at reinforcing what nature may already be asking us to shed.

My Own Molt

Lately, I've been trying to molt something surprisingly ordinary. I realized that I have an almost compulsive need to eliminate silence from conversations. If a pause appears, I rush in with another story, another joke, another observation. I thought I was being a good conversationalist. In truth, I was mostly trying to soothe my own discomfort.

So I've been experimenting with saying less. Not dramatically less. Bird less. A feather here. A feather there. The silence still feels awkward sometimes, and I occasionally catch myself reaching for an unnecessary anecdote the way someone reaches for a familiar sweater. But each time I resist, I notice something unexpected. The conversation doesn't die. Someone else speaks. Or nobody does. Either way, the world continues turning without my plugging up the gaps in the social dialogue.

A Feather at a Time

Birds don't become entirely different birds after they molt. They simply replace what has become worn. They trust that new feathers will grow in their own time. They don't panic because they look a little disheveled for a season.

Maybe we could offer ourselves the same grace. We don't have to reinvent our personalities or emerge as dazzling new versions of ourselves. We only need to notice which old feathers have stopped carrying us. Then, awkwardly and imperfectly, we can let one drift away. The new plumage rarely arrives all at once, but perhaps that's exactly the point. Growth is less often a butterfly than a molt, and maybe looking a little scruffy for a while is one of the surest signs that something new is growing.

item.title: “Maybe It Isn’t That Bad”: The Psychology of Doubting Abuse
item.description:
Domestic Violence

“Maybe It Isn’t That Bad”: The Psychology of Doubting Abuse

Why cognitive dissonance can make abusive behavior harder to recognize.

Posted August 8, 2026

Key points
  • Cognitive dissonance can make survivors question what they know about abuse.
  • This doubt can delay recognition and make it harder for victims to get support.
  • Naming the behavior can be the first step toward recognizing the pattern.

Kathy sat in her car for almost 20 minutes before going inside.

Her partner had screamed at her that morning. He had called her names, told her she was impossible to live with, and threatened to leave her. Later that afternoon, he apologized. He cried. He told her he had been under enormous stress and that he hated himself for the way he had acted. He would change. He would never do it again.

And now Kathy was sitting in the driveway thinking:

He isn't always like this. He really does love me. Maybe I pushed him too far. Maybe I'm making this into something it isn't.

She knew what had happened and remembered vividly how she felt when he had screamed at her. She remembered the full day at work, unable to focus on her project and taking frequent breaks to cry in the bathroom. But sitting in her driveway, the day behind her, the less certain she felt. Her brain was trying desperately to reconcile two things at the same time: I love this person, and this person is hurting me.

So, she got out, and she walked back inside. Again.

Source: Dina Gavrilenko/Pixabay

Cognitive Dissonance Can Make It Harder to Recognize Abuse When It Happens

The psychological conflict Kathy was experiencing has a name: cognitive dissonance. When one's held beliefs or morals clash with reality, this produces a sense of mental discord called cognitive dissonance, which we innately seek to resolve when forced to confront.

For victims weakened by abuse, the easiest way to resolve their cognitive dissonance is by ignoring the behavior and burying the negative emotions that come with it. This is why, like Kathy, so many return to their abuser. Let's explore this more.

Cognitive Dissonance Can Cause Victims to Doubt Their Own Reality

Chronic exposure to fear and stress can affect how the brain processes information, regulates emotion, and makes decisions. When someone has spent months or years in a state of hypervigilance, their cognitive resources may become focused on getting through the immediate threat rather than stepping back and evaluating the relationship objectively.

During the cycle of trauma, the victim’s brain physically changes for the worse in three ways. The amygdala, responsible for regulating fear, learns to stay on heightened alert. This can lead to mood or anxiety disorders. The constant stress also shrinks the total size of both the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex. These regions are responsible for learning new information, planning, and decision making2. As a result, the victim's brain cannot process new information logically, and their attention centers solely on the event or task at hand. In extreme cases, victims lose all interest in dealing with other aspects of life, with depression and anxiety consuming their emotions.

The psychological distress created by this contradiction can intensify anxiety and self-doubt, particularly for someone whose confidence has already been eroded by ongoing abuse. They doubt their own assessments of abusive situations or even their capacity to survive alone1,2. Often, reverting back to the relationship is the only way a victim knows to restore their mental balance. So, they go back, sometimes again and again.

How to Begin Reducing Cognitive Dissonance

Instead of immediately asking, “Am I overreacting?” a survivor can begin by asking, “What actually happened?” Naming the behavior without explaining it away can help create space between the event itself and the story we tell ourselves about why it happened in attempts to excuse or dismiss it.

One way to do this is to ask yourself: “What was happening inside me that made going back feel safer, easier, or more possible than facing the reality of what happened?” Starting to name and validate your reality can help reduce self-doubt.

If you need support for domestic abuse, contact the U.S. National Domestic Violence Hotline at 1-800-799-7233.

Excerpted, in part, from my book Invisible Bruises: How a Better Understanding of the Patterns of Domestic Violence Can Help Survivors Navigate the Legal System.

item.title: Your Partner's Defensiveness Is Not Your Fault
item.description:
Relationships

Your Partner's Defensiveness Is Not Your Fault

When your partner can't empathize, it's not because you didn't explain it right.

Posted August 8, 2026

This post is Part 3 of a series.

In Part 2 of this series, I explored the ways women tend to respond to their partner’s defensiveness and anger. Specifically, I addressed the self-protective but also self-abandoning mechanisms we revert to when we get blindsided by our partner’s reaction to hearing that we were hurt by them. I described the situation where a woman tells her partner that he’s upset her, whether intentionally or unintentionally, and instead of the empathy and understanding she needs, what comes at her is rage and an emotional attack. Women are then quick to assume that they just didn’t phrase their hurt correctly, and not clearly enough for him to understand or empathize with, so it must be her fault that he couldn’t hear her and was so angry. I explained that women tend to jump straight into their assigned role as the perpetrator; when he can’t empathize with her hurt, she becomes the one who hurt him. And from there, she sets out on a mission to “win him back,” jumping through hoops to convince him that he should still love her (despite having wounded him with her experience of him).

There is a path to freedom, however, from these disempowering and self-abandoning behaviors that, in fact, are self-perpetuating and enable the same unkind and unconscious system to keep on rolling. If you want to break free from this pattern that can provide temporary relief but ultimately brings you more pain, I will warn you up front: The path to freedom is not easy and requires a healthy supply of fierce grace. But if you dare to walk it, you will end up in a new place, both inside and outside, a place that’s more truthful and more deeply connected to yourself.

To begin with, when your mind wants to convince you that you need to figure out a better way to explain your hurt, 99 times out of 100, this is false. I guess that you’ve explained this experience to your partner a thousand times in a thousand different ways. You’ve probably reframed, rephrased, and re-analogized why you have a right to be upset in every way imaginable; you’ve probably picked every time of the day and night to address it. The chances are very high that your partner’s reaction has nothing to do with how you worded your truth and everything to do with your partner hearing something they don’t like hearing about themselves. This assumption of responsibility is your fear talking; it’s false evidence appearing real. Underneath the self-blame, you’re afraid of feeling what happened, and what not blaming yourself could mean.

So too, this is your mind trying to find a way to make sense of an experience that doesn’t make any sense and feels so desperately unfair. This narrative that you failed and didn’t use the right words is a way to rationalize the fact that something unimaginable and unspeakably unkind happened. What started as you feeling hurt was weaponized against you, and now you’re left with your original hurt, for which you were hoping to get some comfort, and your partner’s anger and your fear on top of it. Furthermore, you’re left knowing that the empathy you still need is not going to happen. What started out at a level seven on the pain scale has now escalated to an 11 out of 10.

When it comes to the first habit, to self-blame, when your mind tells you that it’s your fault this happened, the answer is straightforward: Tell yourself to “stop!” Or say a simple “enough” to yourself, or maybe “stop doing this to me” (to your mind). Remind yourself of how many different ways you’ve tried to explain why this particular thing hurts, and that your hurt was evident no matter what words were said. If there was any confusion, your partner also has a brain and vocal cords; he can be curious and try to understand if he’s confused. Remind yourself that the fact that you’re hurt is what matters. None of this has to do with finding the right analogy or metaphor that your partner can identify with from his own experience; this is a matter for the heart, not the head. You have to be unrelentingly tough with your own mind here, which, paradoxically, is trying to help you, but isn’t helping you. Remind yourself of all of this with ferocious self-compassion. You’ve done this, you’ve tried this path, it hasn’t worked, and it’s not your fault.

I will address strategies for breaking the second habit—rushing to restore the bond, remove any conflict or discomfort, and essentially convince him to stay with you—in my next post. But spoiler alert, it also involves the word “stop.”
